en: “My stalwart uncle Akjoltoy,
Your strong back is as high as countless troops.
If death arrives and one’s days are done,
Would not even one who attacks me die?
The true land of no return—
Does not everyone journey there and see it?
When a hero desires to ride,
What night is like the sacred Night of Power?
When will the archers
Of the black Chinese and Manchus come?
We were a people who stood shoulder to shoulder;
If the Chinese can be brought to reason,
Without abuse or quarreling,
We shall send them peacefully on their way.
But if the Chinese insult us,
We shall find a way to settle their account.
If they swagger as heroes,
Claiming to be lions greater than us all,
If by chance they glare and bluster,
We shall knock the petty fury from their brows.
If the enemy attacks first,
We shall find a way to settle their account.
If our journey opens a fortunate road,
If my tiger forefather supports me,
If Khidr stands as my guardian,
If the spirits of the champions
Who departed for the other world are with us now,
We shall mount our eager coursers;
If this is a grave and grievous challenge,
If it is an enemy come from China,
We shall drive them all the way to Kakan.
Whether they are foes or peaceful folk,
We shall learn when we meet face-to-face.”
He donned his battle garb,
His gray-wolf valor plain to see;
Unable to remain still in his fervor,
He rode out from the palace.
As he mounted and departed, Akbermet
Spread her palms and sobbed,
Crying helplessly,
Her thoughts scattered a thousand ways,
Her mind racing through the world
As many sorrows rose before her eyes.
The prudent, luckless woman
Brought forth a green-blue coat,
No mere camel-hair coat, but a mighty one:
“Many champions have lifted this;
If you wear it against the enemy, it brings great havoc.
I knew this in my heart,
And saying, ‘Let the champion wear it in battle,’
I had this broad coat made.
Its fastenings are of steel;
For seven full years I had it ceaselessly cut,
And had its rings twisted;
For ninety mighty smiths
I had it hammered ceaselessly
For nine months with mallets.
Cobblers stitched it
With awls made of steel;
At the mere sight of it,
A person’s eyes recoiled.
Lest any hole remain,
An old craftswoman with a brass thimble
Stitched it with such care.
When thrust at with a spear,
The point glanced noisily away without piercing a hair.
Its whole surface was covered in mail,
With lark-eye rings of steel
Set into every part.
It is armor no bullet can pierce,
No spearhead can penetrate,
A coat made for entering battle;
My lion Seytek, put it on,
And rout whichever side you charge.
If a dreadful, perilous road confronts you,
Drive your foe to the ends of the earth;
Remember your poor Perizada
As you go.
The one you will grapple with is a mortal enemy,
And your campaign is a grievous trial;
My leopard, return alive.
My father too was once a khan,
And my poor, valiant father
Possessed treasures of every kind.
The Achalbars sword left by my father—
Its edge never dulled when it struck stone,
And when it hewed through tethered camels,
Its blade never caught or turned.
Its hilt was perfected and fitted
By five smiths descended from fairies,
Who forged it for five or six years.
Unable to endure the labor of its bellows,
Many bulls were slaughtered;
Unable to supply enough charcoal,
A whole forest of green saplings was felled.
Tempered with poison, its edge honed keen,
Forged from the hide of a black male camel,
Its blood-drinking edge put to the test,
The wondrous Ach Albarst, unlike any other—
So the storytellers have sung of it.
If you go to battle, that is the weapon;
If you eagerly confront the foe,
I reckon its thrill is beyond measure.
When you draw it slantwise,
This sword will be your companion till Judgment Day.
When you gloriously drive the enemy back,
Its steel-gray edge turns red.
When you swing it in wrath,
You cleave through ill-fated foes,
And it lengthens to a spear’s reach.
When you brandish it in turmoil,
Your treasure rests secure in your hands;
When you strike the advancing foe,
It will satisfy your laughter.
There were nine pieces of battle armor;
Clad in his battle armor,
The fortunate hero
Revealed the bearing of a tiger.
When he rode against the enemy,
Before that fortunate slayer
The two keen beasts, Koibos and Taibas,
Slunk along ahead,
While the giant black bird Zumuruk,
Stretching out its talons grandly,
Sported high in the sky.
His nine guardian spirits
Were then supporting him.
Taking a shortcut along the narrow path,
The dervish named Khizir
Had taken the hero
And led him by the bridle for a year.
When the destroyer was about to leave the horde,
With the true seer at their head,
Six sorcerers from China
Had come to test the noble one.
The judges who came to test him,
Those who watched from afar,
Would observe tomorrow
His courage and his worth,
How far his strength might reach,
And the full measure of his power,
Then, omitting not a single word,
Would report it to their khan.
Those who watched from afar,
Those who secretly kept watch,
Those charged to deliver a single report,
Those two-eyed magicians,
Those shamans who came from Beijing,
Trusted men of the vast Chinese nation of forty tribes,
Men in whom they placed firm faith,
Men with eyes that watched from afar,
Men skilled in polished words,
Spies who watched in concealment,
Judges who could assess a man—
When Seytek was mounting his horse,
Fastening all his gear,
And Akbermet was being handed to him,
They clearly witnessed the fate
Of the ill-starred Zholtoi.
The two called Dökörchü and Mangi,
Seeing Seytek’s conduct
And grieving at what he did,
Said, “He is a tiger indeed!”
Then both of them died,
Their hearts bursting together.
The spy who meant to observe died,
Saying, “He is truly ill-starred!”
The judge who meant to test him died;
Seeing the gray-maned hero’s deeds,
The watcher standing afar died.
Zhöökülük watched it all—
Zhöökülük stirred up great turmoil,
Fled in frantic confusion,
And Zhöökülük, who had come to test him,
Despaired of his entrusted life.
Of the spies who came to test him,
Five were swallowed by death.
Zhöökülük must have been an extraordinary man,
For he alone escaped without dying.
His reason failed and his senses fled,
And he despaired of his precious life;
Blazing up like a live ember,
Before one could say a word,
In the blink of an eye,
Before anyone could look,
Zhöökülük had crossed
Six ranges and forty hills.
Trembling like a drawn bow,
Hurrying and rushing wildly,
Zhöökülük pressed onward;
In the blink of an eye,
Before anyone could look,
He rushed breathlessly toward Chongbilgich.
Zhöökülük reached him
And stirred up great turmoil.
He spoke of the mighty giant,
Told lies of every kind,
Ranted and exaggerated,
Making them despair of their precious lives,
And so began that lament.
The cauldron that boils men like meat—
The Chinese cast it aside.
Chongbilgich thundered:
“If you know nothing of the people, crawl into the earth!
Though I called you a hero, you are an infidel,
A worthless wretch who ruins the nation;
You go about destroying the people.
These are the very eyes that saw his forefathers;
Now heed these words of mine:
It was our forefather
Who slaughtered the accursed Kyrgyz.
You went scouting, threw the people into disorder,
And spewed crude, corrupt words;
It was you who started this uproar.
Posing as a hero and boasting like a warrior,
You shake the champions’ resolve.
Why do you begin
Such nation-wrecking strife?”
Chongbilgich was indeed a hero:
Does not a man die when his hour comes?
Does he not live while his days remain?
“When he fled at your mere words,
His noble father, Kojozhash,
Had only just seen this son born before he died.
Will they not say he fled back here,
Without a shadow of courage or a word to speak?
Will they not say he came fleeing in panic,
Scattering all his possessions?
Will they not say all six lost their wits
And perished?
Will they not say you came here
Embroidering your tale with wild exaggeration?
If you are no swift-footed runner, crawl into the earth!
Who should listen to these words of yours?
Let the blinding night hear them;
Let the muddy water hear them,
Let empty shrieks and clamor hear them.
Know now what I tell you:
Bury yourself in the earth along with your words.
As for the measure of this tale of yours,
Let the dog barking at the bөө hear it,
Let the birdlike beast called bөө hear it—
Who else but these should listen?
Yesterday, when your mother labored and bore you,
The people must have gathered and the nation rejoiced,
Saying, ‘A son has been born!’
They must have given countless rams and livestock
As rewards for the glad tidings,
Calling you a man who would uphold honor,
And saying you would defend the people.
Fail to guard the people and be ruined!
Fail to be a man and die!
You have spoken words that kindle panic;
Hey, would that you had sunk away unborn!
You have terrified my people,
And bent my back beneath the burden.
